turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come in, have a seat. What brings you in today?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, Doctor. I have had pain in the jaw when I chew, and I felt I ought to have it seen to.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mm. Which side is it, and how long has it been bothering you?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): The right side. It has been three weeks, umm, no, closer to five weeks. After a chewy meal I feel as though I have overdone it.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does the jaw click, or lock, or is it only an ache?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): It clicks when I open wide. It does not lock, I am pleased to say.
[SEG0007] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Sorry to cut in. I live with him, we are partners. I have heard him grinding his teeth most nights for weeks.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): I was not aware of that myself. I am sorry if it has been a nuisance at night.

[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me think it through out loud. Pain on chewing, a click, and night grinding fits the jaw joint and the chewing muscles, and a cracked tooth can imitate it. I am not going to conclude this is arthritis today.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): I understand, and I would rather you did not rush to a label.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fever with this?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No, no fever. I have felt quite well in myself, apart from being tired.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tired how?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): By the evening I feel like a wet rag, if you will forgive the phrase. The days are rather long.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. Is the click with every bite, or only when you open wide?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Mainly with a wide opening, or with crusty bread. Not with every mouthful.
[SEG0017] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The grinding gets louder when work has been grim. Nearly every night lately, I would say.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does stress make the pain worse, or only the grinding?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): The pain is worse when I am under pressure. At the open-plan office I cannot hear myself think, though that is the building noise and not my hearing.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Of. I will not treat that as an ear symptom. Any ear pain, or any swelling you have seen?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): No ear pain, and no swelling that I have noticed.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): What have you been taking for the ache?

[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Neurofen. I thought the tablets were two hundred milligrams, uh, but I checked the packet and they are four hundred. I take one by mouth when it is bad, perhaps twice a day.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything else regular?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing else.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any allergies, medicines or otherwise?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): None that I am aware of.

[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): I will have a feel. Open slowly. There is a click on the right as you open, and the muscle just in front of the ear is tender. There is no swelling, and you open about three fingers, which is acceptable.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): It is a little tender there, yes. Some mornings I have a frog in my throat, though it clears once I have had tea.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): A rough voice, or pain in the throat?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Only a rough voice, for a few minutes. Nothing more than that.
[SEG0032] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He also says his feet feel dead after standing about. I am not sure he means it medically.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): I would not wish to mislead you. They are not numb. They are simply weary after a long day on my feet.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thank you, that is fatigue rather than numbness. Any cough, wheeze, or trouble with your breathing?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing of that sort.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): What is the work, in that open-plan office?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): I am a conveyancing solicitor. The hours have been heavy this quarter, I am afraid.
[SEG0038] person_3 (CAREGIVER): We share a flat in Carlton, so I hear the night grinding more than he realises.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke, or, err, take a drink in the evenings?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): I have never smoked. I have a glass of wine with dinner, perhaps four nights a week.

[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): My working impression is temporomandibular joint dysfunction driven by the night grinding. A dental cause is still possible, so I would like a dentist to exclude a tooth problem.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): I shall arrange to see one. What should I do in the meantime?

[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): A soft diet for the next fortnight, no crusty bread and no steak, and a boil-and-bite mouth guard from the chemist at night until the dentist advises. Keep the neurofen at four hundred milligrams, up to twice a day, with food.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, Doctor. That is very clear.

[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): If it has not eased in a fortnight, come back and see me. If the jaw locks or you develop a fever, do not wait, and reception can give you a dentist's name on the way out.

spec.situation: Person with jaw pain on chewing and clicking, worse with stress, teeth grinding noticed by partner; no fever; mouth guard and soft diet advice.

traps.happens: The patient describes things in colourful or sentence-like speech ('I've overdone it', 'I can't hear myself think', 'a frog in my throat', 'my feet feel dead', 'I feel like a wet rag').
traps.label_rule: Every symptom name is a short clinical noun phrase of 1 to 5 words ('voice fatigue', 'numbness in both feet', 'tiredness'), never a full sentence, never starting with I/we/my. Pure idioms that are not symptoms ('I can't hear myself think' said about classroom noise) are NOT symptoms. The patient's own words stay in the cited turn, not in the name.

features: doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.
